# Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems

Erkang Zhu Affiliation: Alibaba Research Correspondence to:
<erkang.zhu@alibaba-inc.com>    Yin Lin Affiliation: Alibaba Research
Correspondence to: <yin.lin@alibaba-inc.com>    Xiaorong Shi
Affiliation: Alibaba Research Correspondence to:
<shixiaorong.sxr@alibaba-inc.com>    Xuanrui Lin Affiliation: Alibaba
Research Correspondence to: <linxuanrui.lxr@alibaba-inc.com>    Jingren
Zhou Affiliation: Alibaba Research Correspondence to:
<jingren.zhou@alibaba-inc.com>

###### Abstract

Foundation models in changing environments can encounter unfamiliar
domain knowledge that their original training did not cover. However,
new domains rarely provide large amounts of expert-created training data
or reliable supervisory signals for further training.

We introduce Recursa, a foundation model system that adapts to new
domains by learning from its own experience without human experts or a
stronger teacher model. Recursa uses a knowledge repository to store
what it learns: domain-specific skills and instructions on when to apply
them, along with memories of past task experiences and reflections on
what to improve. Recursa bootstraps the repository from domain materials
and then refines it through recursive self-improvement. It uses parallel
learners to execute tasks and synthesize local improvements, then
validates and merges the improvements into the knowledge repository. On
Harvey LAB’s Firm Knowledge benchmark, Recursa raises the all-pass rate
on held-out test tasks from 30.0% to 55.0% with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and
from 35.0% to 46.0% with Qwen3.8-Flash.

## 1 Introduction

| Phase                      | Primary signals                                              | Objective                                                                                                                                                                         |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Bootstrapping              | Domain materials and self-practice tasks generated from them | Close the knowledge gap: summarize and map the materials and practice applying them, with parallel agents covering the materials.                                                 |
| Recursive self-improvement | Training tasks, execution traces, and available feedback     | Close the behavior gap: refine the knowledge repository from task experience by decomposing learning across child learners, attempting tasks in parallel, and validating results. |

Table 1: Recursa’s learning phases.

A foundation model is trained across diverse domains, yet it will always
encounter new knowledge, unseen requirements, and unfamiliar tools in a
changing environment. Adapting the model through further training, such
as reinforcement learning, requires extensive training data and reliable
supervision or reward signals, which a new domain rarely provides at
first. The model’s instructions, skills, memory, and harness, on the
other hand, can be learned directly from domain materials and task
experience. The accumulated knowledge in these components, in turn,
provides data for training the model. Therefore, domain adaptation means
learning the whole system, not just the model. The challenge, then, is
not just to train a strong model once, but to build a foundation model
system that continues to acquire knowledge and adapt its behavior.

We call this problem _foundation model system learning_: improving a
system comprising a model, instructions, skills, memory, and a harness
through domain materials and task experience. Learning must close two
gaps. The knowledge gap arises when the system lacks the domain’s facts,
terminology, or knowledge of where its materials are located. The
behavior gap arises when the system has the required information but
applies it incorrectly; for example, it may find the relevant documents
yet select the wrong ones when writing an answer. To close the knowledge
gap, the system can learn from the domain’s materials; to close the
behavior gap, it can learn by working on tasks and reflecting on
feedback. We study the setting in which the system recursively
self-improves: the system’s own model modifies the system to address
both gaps and refine the improvement process itself, without help from a
human expert or a stronger model.

Knowledge-intensive domains such as law and finance make this problem
harder. The domain knowledge is scattered and lacks a common
organization, and behavioral expectations are highly local: the same
evidence may support different conclusions depending on the context and
the user’s objectives, and correctness is often difficult to verify
automatically. This requires an efficient learning method capable of
drawing on more materials and task experience than any one agent can
examine. This also requires a harness that can sustain long-horizon work
for the same model in both roles: finding evidence among thousands of
documents to solve a task, and diagnosing and reflecting on failures
across many long agent trajectories to improve the learning process.

Existing methods learn parts of the system: its instructions ([Khattab
et al., 2024](#bib.bib23); [Yuksekgonul et al., 2025](#bib.bib24);
[Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Zhang et al., 2026d](#bib.bib30)),
harness ([Cheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib25); [Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib31); [Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib8); [Zhang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib17); [Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib27); [Zheng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib18)), tools, skills, and subagents ([Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib28); [Lin et al., 2026a](#bib.bib34); [Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib29); [Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)), the learning method
itself ([Zelikman et al., 2024](#bib.bib16); [Zhang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib32); [Ye et al., 2026](#bib.bib33); [Lee et al.,
2026](#bib.bib27); [Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)), or foundation
models ([Hebbar et al., 2026](#bib.bib35); [Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib37)). Most of these methods learn how to act from task
feedback, targeting the behavior gap. In contrast, methods that limit
themselves to studying a domain corpus ([Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib9);
[Sun et al., 2026](#bib.bib13); [Engram, 2026](#bib.bib6)) target the
knowledge gap. Incorporating domain knowledge and applying it correctly,
however, requires addressing both gaps. In-context reflection on task
feedback ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib7)) learns from linguistic
feedback without updating weights, but keeps its reflections within a
single task’s retries rather than accumulating them across tasks.
Moreover, most existing methods are evaluated on coding, mathematics,
and games. In those domains, evaluation often focuses on short, exact
answers that do not check supporting evidence or reasoning behind the
answers, or on numerical metrics that allow repeated self-testing and
refinement on the same task. Often, these methods also rely on a
stronger model to drive learning ([Yuksekgonul et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24); [Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib8); [Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib31)), rather than using the system’s own model to
self-improve.

We introduce Recursa, a foundation model system that adapts to new
domains through recursive self-improvement. Recursa stores what it
learns in a knowledge repository of instructions, skills, and memory
that the model draws on when solving tasks and improving the system
itself.

Recursa bootstraps the knowledge repository by summarizing and mapping
domain materials and practicing on tasks generated from them, thereby
closing the knowledge gap. It then refines the repository through task
experience to close the behavior gap
(Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")).
The same model bootstraps, solves, and learns iteratively. Each
iteration updates the knowledge repository and changes how the model
acts as a solver as well as a learner. This cycle lets the system
improve on its own rather than relying on guidance from a stronger
model. Both phases distribute work across parallel agents and merge
their results, enabling them to process larger amounts of domain
material and diverse task experience. All agents run on a harness built
for long-horizon work
(Section [3](#S3 "3 Harness ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")).

The accumulated learning in the knowledge repository becomes the source
of training data for model learning and harness improvement. In this
paper, we focus on learning the knowledge repository that forms the
basis for a fully recursively self-improving foundation model system.

We evaluate Recursa on Harvey LAB’s Firm Knowledge benchmark ([Harvey
AI, 2026](#bib.bib14)), where the correctness of a long-form answer
depends on specific knowledge and its accurate application. We found
that the harness alone provides a strong starting point. Bootstrapping
makes each task attempt more efficient, and recursive self-improvement
enables the system to complete substantially more tasks: without a
stronger model revising it, Recursa raises its all-pass rate on held-out
test tasks from 30.0% to 55.0% with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and from 35.0%
to 46.0% with Qwen3.8-Flash.

## 2 Recursa: A Multi-Agent Learning System

Recursa adapts to a new domain using multiple agents working together.
This section defines the agent roles and the learnable components.

### 2.1 Agents

Recursa assigns task execution and recursive self-improvement to two
agent roles, both running on the harness described in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Harness ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems").
Solvers execute domain tasks using the current learnable components
$`K`$
(Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Learnable Components ‣ 2 Recursa: A Multi-Agent Learning System ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")).
Given a task $`x`$, a solver searches the environment, gathers evidence,
and returns an answer $`y`$ and execution trace $`\tau`$:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       (y,\ \tau)=\textsc{Solve}(x,\ K).
       ```                                |     | (1) |

Learners improve the solver’s components. Given tasks $`D`$ and starting
components $`K`$, a learner calls solvers, inspects their answers,
execution traces, and available feedback, and uses them to develop and
validate revisions of the solver’s components. Alternatively, it
decomposes the learning task into subtasks and assigns them to child
learners, for example by dividing $`D`$ among them. It validates and
merges their revisions, then reflects on the children’s learning traces
and stores those reflections in memory to guide future learning
(Section [5](#S5 "5 Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")).
It returns the revised components $`K^{\prime}`$ and a learning trace
$`\mathcal{T}`$:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       (K^{\prime},\ \mathcal{T})=\textsc{Learn}(D,\ K).
       ```                                                |     | (2) |

The learning trace contains the learner’s actions, the execution traces
of its solvers, and its children’s learning traces.

### 2.2 Learnable Components

A foundation model system’s learnable components fall into three groups:

- •
  Knowledge repository: what the system knows about a domain and how to
  apply it.
  - –
    Instructions: the system prompt, guardrails, and other guidance in
    the context at every step.
  - –
    Skills: reusable packages of procedural knowledge loaded on demand,
    following the Agent Skills format ([Agent Skills,
    2025](#bib.bib22)); each holds instructions and may bundle scripts
    and reference materials.
  - –
    Memory: reflections that learners record on past task executions and
    learning experiences, such as categories of failure cases and
    different strategies for addressing them.

- •
  Harness: how the system executes and learns. It comprises the loop
  that executes the models’ actions and manages their context
  (Section [3](#S3 "3 Harness ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")),
  the tools available to agents, and subagents, which take a main text
  input and run an agent in an isolated sandbox with its own
  instructions, skills, and tools.
- •
  Foundation models: models capable of following instructions, using
  tools, and reasoning through long chains of thought. Each agent and
  subagent is configured with its own model.

Among these components, the natural starting point is the knowledge
repository because it can be updated and used immediately on the next
task. Also, because it is represented in text, it can be easily checked
against the source materials. Model learning builds on the knowledge
repository by training foundation models to internalize the knowledge it
captures. In this paper’s setup, Recursa learns only its knowledge
repository, so the learnable components $`K`$ are its instructions,
skills, and memory; the harness and the models stay fixed. Learning them
is future work.

In our setting, a new domain provides a corpus of materials, such as
documents, code, or raw data, and a set of training tasks $`D`$, with
feedback on task execution. Recursa first bootstraps its knowledge
repository from the corpus
(Section [4](#S4 "4 Bootstrapping Domain Knowledge ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")),
then iteratively refines it by learning from $`D`$
(Section [5](#S5 "5 Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")).

## 3 Harness

The harness is the layer that turns a foundation model into an agent.
Recursa’s harness enables the model to act in code: at each step, the
model writes an action in Python, and the harness executes it in a
persistent Python read-eval-print loop (REPL), returns selected output
to the model’s context, and appends the step to a persistent event log
(Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Harness ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")).
The harness also connects the knowledge repository to the model: it
loads instructions and skills into the model’s context. For learners,
the harness also loads into the context the memory that records
reflections from earlier learning. Tools are loaded into the REPL as
callable functions. Subagents are also callable from the REPL; each call
dispatches an agent to work in an isolated sandbox and returns its
result. Solvers and learners run on the same harness with different
levels of access to the knowledge repositories.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: Recursa’s harness. The model writes Python code, the REPL
executes it, and its output returns to the context. The context is
appended to the event log, which the REPL queries. Recursa learns the
knowledge repository (orange) in this paper; the harness and the
foundation models stay fixed.

Recursa’s harness design rests on three features that make it effective
over long horizons: tool composition, programmatic context management,
and multi-agent orchestration. They support the system’s tools, history,
and subagents, respectively. The harness supports both solvers and
learners. It provides a strong starting point before any adaptation
(Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Harness: Tool Composition and Context Management ‣ 6 Experiments on Harvey LAB ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")).

Figure 2: Recursa’s harness. (a) The agent composes tools in persistent
REPL cells; intermediate results such as docs stay in Python, and only
the verified excerpt returns to the model. (b) Past interactions live in
an append-only event log; the agent retrieves them in code, and only
selected evidence enters the active context.

### 3.1 Tool Composition

In a typical ReAct-style agent ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib36)), each
operation is a separate tool call, every intermediate result passes
through the model’s context, and steps such as filtering and aggregation
span across multiple model calls. In contrast, Recursa’s harness builds
on code-based tool use ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Jones and
Kelly, 2025](#bib.bib2); [Jaghouar, 2026](#bib.bib20)): the agent
interacts with a persistent REPL that exposes document search, file
access, and external APIs as callable libraries.

The agent composes tools with programming primitives such as loops,
conditionals, and functions. Intermediate results remain in variables,
and only selected output is returned to the model. The harness truncates
long outputs and saves them to disk ([SST, 2026](#bib.bib21)), and on
errors returns stack traces that inform the next action. Retaining
variables in REPL allows for retrying failed steps without repeating
successful ones. In
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Harness ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")a,
one REPL cell searches for candidate agreements and a second one reuses
the stored docs to verify a no-shop clause; only the verified excerpt
reaches the model’s context.

### 3.2 Programmatic Context Management

Learning requires recalling earlier interactions, such as the tool
result that led to an incorrect conclusion. However, keeping the
complete history in the model’s limited context is infeasible over long
horizons. Recursa keeps the full interaction history outside the model’s
context in a persistent, append-only event log and lets an agent use
code and to retrieve records into REPL variables, following the approach
of Scroll ([Lin et al., 2026b](#bib.bib3)). The model context holds only
recent history and an eviction index that tracks ranges of removed
records that can be retrieved via log addresses. In
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Harness ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")b,
the solver agent recovers earlier no-shop evidence by searching the
event log in code, and only the selected clause enters the model
context. Across solver attempts, a learner agent likewise assembles
records for diagnosis without reloading the complete solver traces.

### 3.3 Multi-Agent Orchestration

Even with programmatic context management, some tasks are too large or
complex for a single agent. Such tasks often involve multiple branches
of work and rich substructures that naturally decompose into
subproblems—for example, surveying a large corpus or diagnosing hundreds
of failure cases. Recursa’s harness supports multi-agent orchestration:
an agent dispatches subagents to process parts of the workload in
parallel and merges their findings, following Recursive Language
Models ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib4)) and their application to M&A
diligence ([Grupen et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)).

## 4 Bootstrapping Domain Knowledge

An agent entering a new environment does not know what it contains, how
it is organized, which conventions it follows, or where its boundaries
lie. The environment may be a document collection, a codebase, a
database, or a set of tools and services. Without an understanding of
the environment, every task begins with exploration. This cost compounds
in a learning system with multiple agents (e.g., repeated solver
attempts by different agents). To reduce repeated exploration, Recursa
begins domain adaptation by bootstrapping its knowledge repository from
the domain corpus.

### 4.1 Products of Bootstrapping

Bootstrapping records its findings as skills in a form that solvers and
learners can navigate. Two forms suit different environments.

##### Navigation structures

suit large and heterogeneous collections. Summaries are linked to source
locations, and structured metadata (entities, document types, status,
and dates) narrows search to relevant regions of the corpus. This design
follows the multi-level summaries of RAPTOR ([Sarthi et al.,
2024](#bib.bib10)) and the navigable hierarchies of Corpus2Skill ([Sun
et al., 2026](#bib.bib13)). The organization follows the environment
rather than a fixed taxonomy.

##### Exploration notes

suit narrower, well-structured domains, such as a single software
project. They record terminology, conventions, and guidance for future
investigation in a compact cheatsheet, following self-written
cheatsheets for software libraries ([Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib15)).

In both forms, every entry retains a link to its source and states its
uncertainty and applicable scope, so solvers and learners can determine
when to trust an entry and when to consult the original sources.
Bootstrapping also records the boundaries of the environment: which
kinds of material are present, which are absent, and which are covered
only partially. This information does not replace the original sources,
and entries can be revised as later experience accumulates.

##### Bootstrapping with multiple agents.

For a large corpus, a single agent may struggle to process all the
materials. Recursa uses multi-agent orchestration
(Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Multi-Agent Orchestration ‣ 3 Harness ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems"))
to dispatch parallel agents over portions of the corpus. Each agent
summarizes and maps its portion in depth, and an orchestrating agent
merges their findings into skills, checks them against the sources, and
assigns follow-up work.

### 4.2 Self-Practice

To turn domain materials into experience for learning, agents generate
practice tasks grounded in those materials. SPICE generates reasoning
tasks from documents through challenger–reasoner self-play ([Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib11)), while PREPING builds procedural memory from
validated synthetic practice before target tasks are observed ([Choi et
al., 2026](#bib.bib12)).

Recursa similarly generates practice tasks from the materials read
during bootstrapping and uses the resulting experience to refine the
initial skills. Tasks require agents to find relevant sources, reconcile
evidence, and produce supported responses. Learners assess the attempts,
examine the evidence and decisions behind successes and failures, record
their reflections in memory, and update the skills with knowledge or
strategies that can improve future performance. Practice records retain
source references so that proposed lessons can be checked against the
materials. Sparse guidance, such as preferences, example rubrics, or
known failure modes, can steer task generation and assessment toward
relevant behaviors.

Corpus exploration and self-practice produce the initial skills and
memory in the bootstrapped components $`K^{(0)}`$, the starting point
for recursive self-improvement from training tasks and their feedback
(Section [5](#S5 "5 Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")).

## 5 Recursive Self-Improvement

Recursa’s recursive self-improvement involves repeated task solving and
failure diagnosis, followed by editing and validating its learnable
components for use in subsequent attempts. Learners improve solver
performance by refining its instructions and skills, while the learners
accumulate reflections in memory to guide future improvements.

Starting from the bootstrapped components $`K^{(0)}`$, Recursa refines
them by calling $`\textsc{Learn}(D,K^{(0)})`$ on the training tasks
$`D`$
(Equation [2](#S2.E2 "In 2.1 Agents ‣ 2 Recursa: A Multi-Agent Learning System ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")).
A learner can split its tasks into subsets and call a child learner on
each
(Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Decomposition, Merging, and Reflection ‣ 5 Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems"));
a _leaf learner_, which does not split, refines the components directly
in a self-improvement loop with parallel solvers.
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5 Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")
shows the structure, and
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 5 Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")
summarizes it. We write $`K^{(t)}`$ for the components after round $`t`$
of the top-level learner, where a round is one iteration of its loop;
subscripts such as $`K_{i}`$ index child learners.

### 5.1 Leaf Learner: The Self-Improvement Loop

A leaf learner calls solvers directly and produces revisions to the
solver’s components. It repeats four steps:

- •
  Solve. Dispatch solvers in parallel, one per task in $`D`$, each using
  the current components $`K`$.
- •
  Diagnose. Read the feedback and execution traces of failed attempts,
  separate genuine solver errors from noisy or ambiguous feedback,
  identify missing knowledge or behavior, and reflect on previous edits.
- •
  Edit. Refine the instructions and skills to address the diagnosed
  errors, drawing on previous reflections.
- •
  Validate. Solve the affected tasks again, together with a sample of
  tasks that already passed, and keep an edit only if it fixes failures
  without causing regressions.

The loop stops when no edit improves the results or the budget is spent.

### 5.2 Decomposition, Merging, and Reflection

##### Splitting.

A learner decides whether to split $`D`$ and how. It can split the tasks
by category, such as topic or document type; by failure case, grouping
tasks that fail in the same way; by the skill that each subset should
improve; or by the tools that each subset practices. The aim is to
minimize duplicate work: when subsets exercise different skills,
children are less likely to diagnose the same failure twice or rework
the same skills, and their edits cause fewer conflicts when merged. The
learner issues a learning task $`(D_{i},K)`$ to a child learner for each
subset $`D_{i}`$. Children run in parallel and may split their subsets
further.

##### Merging.

Each child returns its own revision $`K_{i}`$ of the components. The
parent merges these revisions into a single set of components: it
removes duplicates, reconciles conflicting edits, and generalizes
lessons that recur across subsets. It then solves a sample of the
children’s tasks with the merged components to check that merging did
not undo their gains.

##### Reflection.

The parent reads the children’s learning traces $`\mathcal{T}_{1:c}`$ to
find subsets that did not improve, edits that conflicted, and tasks
whose feedback appears unreliable. Based on this reflection, it issues
new learning tasks that start from the merged components, possibly over
different subsets. It repeats until no further progress is made or the
budget is spent; its learning trace includes the children’s traces.

### 5.3 Learning Waste and Learning Signal

Two considerations guide how learners split, solve, and edit: reducing
learning waste and making better use of the learning signal.

##### Reducing learning waste.

_Learning waste_ is time or compute spent without advancing learning. It
takes two forms. _Stalls_ occur when agents, including learners and
solvers, are idle: they do no work while waiting for dependencies or
results. _Rework_ is repeated, redundant work, such as rereading
unchanged state, rediscovering the directory layout, or reinvestigating
a failure that another learner has already diagnosed. Stalls consume
wall-clock time, while rework also consumes active compute. Running
children and solvers in parallel reduces stalls, and splitting tasks so
that subsets exercise different skills can reduce rework
(Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Decomposition, Merging, and Reflection ‣ 5 Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")).
Excessive splitting, however, creates merge conflicts and duplicate
investigations across children. A learner revises its own approach to
both forms of waste by analyzing its learning trace to identify
inefficiencies; it can find stalls and rework in its own trace and
change how it splits, solves, and edits. The learner stores these
reflections in memory, which informs future decisions and helps reduce
both stalls and rework for subsequent learning tasks.

##### Making better use of the learning signal.

The _learning signal_ is the feedback that drives revisions to the
components. _Solver signals_ come from task attempts: the feedback on
each answer and the execution trace $`\tau`$ behind it. _Learner
signals_ come from the learning process itself: validation outcomes,
checks against sources, and the learning traces of child learners.
Solver signals are often noisy, so a learner uses solver signals
iteratively to refine its diagnoses. Each round of calling solvers adds
experience that confirms or overturns earlier diagnoses, helps separate
genuine solver errors from noisy feedback, and sharpens the next
revision. Reflections recorded in memory carry these diagnoses from one
round to the next.

## 6 Experiments on Harvey LAB

| Agent setup                                     | Criteria pass | All-pass |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------- | -------- |
| Reference base agent (no study)                 | 58.2%         | 21.6%    |
| Reference agent after study (high study effort) | 70.1%         | 31.0%    |
| Our harness (persistent REPL), original rubrics | 78.9%         | 35.2%    |
| Our harness (persistent REPL), revised rubrics  | 79.1%         | 37.2%    |

Evaluation and adaptation procedures differ across systems.

Table 2: Task performance with Qwen3.8-27B across agent setups. The
reference rows report the base agent without study and the
highest-accuracy study configuration from the published
evaluation ([Engram, 2026](#bib.bib6)). Our setup uses a persistent REPL
and is scored by Qwen3.8-Max with the original and the revised rubrics
(Section [6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 6 Experiments on Harvey LAB ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")).

Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) is an open-source benchmark that
evaluates agents on realistic, long-horizon legal work. Its _Firm
Knowledge_ environment models a synthetic law firm comprising 46
fictional clients, 266 matters across 15 practice areas, 9,288 files,
and approximately 108 million tokens ([Harvey AI, 2026](#bib.bib14)).¹¹
1 We use the Firm Knowledge tasks and rubrics from the harvey-labs
repository at commit b22bccffd2a496ffc871ffdd1514cde194034071 (v1.2.0).
The benchmark contains 250 tasks that require agents to search across
the full corpus, identify relevant matters and source documents, reason
over evidence distributed across multiple files, and produce a long-form
answer that satisfies task-specific rubric criteria.

The environment is deliberately challenging. Relevant evidence is
scattered across several documents, literal keyword matching is
insufficient, and successful completion depends on finding plausible
evidence and determining whether it is complete, current, and relevant.
Strong performance therefore requires more than document retrieval. The
agent must possess knowledge of firm-specific practices and the judgment
to apply it. Much of this workspace-specific knowledge and practice is
initially unavailable to the model, making the benchmark a natural
setting for studying domain adaptation.

We use this benchmark to investigate three related questions: how a
harness can support tool use and context management; what reusable
knowledge an agent can acquire by bootstrapping from the corpus; and
whether subsequent task experience can further improve the learnable
components.

### 6.1 Experimental Setup

For the harness evaluation
(Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Harness: Tool Composition and Context Management ‣ 6 Experiments on Harvey LAB ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")),
we use Qwen3.8-27B as the solver to match the published reference. For
bootstrapping and self-improvement, we run Recursa with two models,
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash, each serving as both solver and
learner. We report two primary metrics. _Mean criteria pass rate_
measures the fraction of rubric criteria satisfied for each task,
averaged across tasks, while _all-pass rate_ measures strict end-to-end
task success, requiring all rubric criteria for a task to be satisfied.
We use Qwen3.8-Max to judge every criterion in all experiments. We split
the 250 tasks into 150 training and 100 test tasks, stratified by the
per-task criteria pass rate of Qwen3.8-27B before learning, so that both
sets have similar difficulty.

We found 46 criteria in 30 tasks that conflict with the task statement
or with the source documents. For example, a criterion accepts only an
internal memo as evidence and rejects the executed agreement, which
records the same fact; or an enumerated answer set omits matters that
satisfy the task. We revised these criteria and leave the task
statements, criterion IDs, and the other 220 tasks unchanged
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Revisions to the Firm Knowledge Rubrics ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")).
Table [2](#S6.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 6 Experiments on Harvey LAB ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")
and
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Results of Every Round ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")
report results under both rubrics; the revisions raise most scores by up
to four points and lower only one by one point. Unless stated otherwise,
we report the revised rubrics.

### 6.2 Harness: Tool Composition and Context Management

We evaluate Recursa’s harness
(Section [3](#S3 "3 Harness ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")),
which uses a persistent Python REPL to compose tools programmatically
and keep intermediate results out of the model’s context. Its context
management retrieves earlier interactions on demand. Without learning,
the harness establishes a strong baseline: using the same model, it
achieves higher scores than both the base agent and the highest-accuracy
study configuration in the published evaluation ([Engram,
2026](#bib.bib6))
(Table [2](#S6.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 6 Experiments on Harvey LAB ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")).
Evaluation and adaptation procedures differ across systems.

### 6.3 Bootstrapping: Learning the Workspace

Figure 4: Effect of bootstrapping with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on all 250
tasks, scored with the revised rubrics. Teal bars show the baseline;
orange-brown bars show the bootstrapped components (14 skills), after
building the navigation structure from the raw corpus and practicing on
self-generated tasks. Input tokens are totals accumulated across all
turns of a task, averaged over tasks (M: million tokens).

Bootstrapping prepares the agent from domain materials
(Section [4](#S4 "4 Bootstrapping Domain Knowledge ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")).
On Harvey LAB, Recursa first builds a navigation structure over the
firm’s corpus of legal matters, then practices on self-generated tasks.
The resulting components contain 14 skills: a navigation skill that
relates each of the 266 matters to notes and underlying source
documents, and 13 skills distilled from practice. These cover topics
such as determining a task’s scope from matter identifiers, tracing
version chains, and verifying numbers and dates against conflicting
sources. The navigation skill helps the agent identify promising regions
of the corpus without repeating broad searches for every task.

Figure [4](#S6.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 6.3 Bootstrapping: Learning the Workspace ‣ 6 Experiments on Harvey LAB ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")
compares the baseline with the bootstrapped components on all 250 tasks.
Bootstrapping reduces both interaction turns and input tokens by roughly
a fifth to a quarter and raises the all-pass rate slightly, while the
mean criteria pass rate remains unchanged.

The small accuracy gain is consistent with the strong baseline
performance before bootstrapping. Without corpus knowledge, the agent
can spend more turns searching the corpus and composing queries, making
up for missing workspace knowledge as it locates relevant sources.
Corpus knowledge shortens this search, so its main role is to reduce the
search and context costs of each solver attempt.

### 6.4 Self-Improvement on Training Tasks

|                          |             |          |            |          |
| ------------------------ | ----------- | -------- | ---------- | -------- |
|                          | Train (150) |          | Test (100) |          |
| Components               | All-pass    | Criteria | All-pass   | Criteria |
| _DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash_    |             |          |            |          |
| No learning              | 32.0        | 79.8     | 30.0       | 80.0     |
| Bootstrap                | 34.7        | 80.6     | 33.0       | 78.9     |
| Learning, single learner | 34.7        | 75.3     | 43.0       | 78.8     |
| Learning, multi-learner  | 48.7        | 86.3     | 55.0       | 84.1     |
| _Qwen3.8-Flash_          |             |          |            |          |
| No learning              | 35.3        | 80.6     | 35.0       | 83.2     |
| Bootstrap                | 37.3        | 83.2     | 34.0       | 80.5     |
| Learning, single learner | 30.0        | 73.1     | 37.0       | 77.7     |
| Learning, multi-learner  | 47.3        | 85.6     | 46.0       | 84.4     |

Table 3: Results on Harvey LAB with the revised rubrics (all-pass rate
and mean criteria pass rate, %). _No learning_: the harness without
learned components. _Bootstrap_: the components from bootstrapping.
_Learning_: the components from self-improvement, starting from the
bootstrapped components. The single learner reports $`K^{(4)}`$ with
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and $`K^{(5)}`$ with Qwen3.8-Flash. Multi-learner
learning reports $`K^{(2)}`$ with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, from merged
per-subset components and one further round, and $`K^{(1)}`$ with
Qwen3.8-Flash, from merging per-subset components learned on all 150
training tasks.

This experiment examines how Recursa converts task experience into
improved legal research expertise. Starting from the bootstrapped
components, Recursa calls Learn
(Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 5 Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems"))
with $`D`$ set to all 150 training tasks.

The top-level learner splits the tasks by topic into subsets, such as
banking and finance terms, credit precedents, capital-markets offering
documents, and M&A agreement terms. Then it assigns each subset to a
leaf learner, which runs the self-improvement loop over its assigned
subset. The top-level learner then collects the resulting revisions from
each subset and merges them into a single component, $`K^{(1)}`$ (32
skills with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash), then runs four more rounds of the
self-improvement loop on all 150 training tasks, revising the merged
components into $`K^{(2)}`$ through $`K^{(5)}`$.

Table [3](#S6.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 6.4 Self-Improvement on Training Tasks ‣ 6 Experiments on Harvey LAB ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")
reports the results. With DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, the multi-learner
components $`K^{(2)}`$ raises the training all-pass rate from 34.7%
after bootstrapping to 48.7% and the test all-pass rate from 33.0% to
55.0%, 25 percentage points above the agent without learning. The merged
components $`K^{(1)}`$ score higher on the training tasks (51.3%) and
lower on the test tasks (48.0%);
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Results of Every Round ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")
reports every round. With Qwen3.8-Flash, the merged components
$`K^{(1)}`$ raise the training all-pass rate from 37.3% to 47.3% and the
test all-pass rate from 34.0% to 46.0%, 11 percentage points above the
agent without learning. With both solvers, gains concentrate in all-pass
rate: learning converts partially correct answers into complete
successes, and these gains carry over to test tasks that never informed
learning.

##### Single-learner baseline.

To isolate the effect of multiple learners, we compare against a single
leaf learner
(Section [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Leaf Learner: The Self-Improvement Loop ‣ 5 Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems"))
that runs the self-improvement loop with parallel solvers on all 150
training tasks, without splitting. The learner and solvers use the same
model as in the multi-learner runs, and the learner starts from the same
bootstrapped components. We run it for five rounds with each solver.
With DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, the single learner’s $`K^{(4)}`$ reaches
all-pass rates of 34.7% on the training tasks and 43.0% on the test
tasks, below the 48.7% and 55.0% achieved by multi-learner learning.
With Qwen3.8-Flash, the single learner’s $`K^{(5)}`$ falls below the
bootstrap baseline in training all-pass rate (30.0% versus 37.3%), and
its test all-pass rate reaches 37.0%, versus 46.0% for multi-learner
learning.

### 6.5 Learned Domain Judgment

Figure 5: Q157, a test task, with Qwen3.8-Flash: reading covenants by
substance leads to a more recent qualifying agreement. Rows compare
search behavior, verification, and the selected transaction and signing
date. Traces are paraphrased.

Figure 6: Q078, a test task, with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: engagement
records define the candidate scope before settlements are checked. The
returned set changes from eight matters to the seven qualifying matters.
Traces are paraphrased.

Learning changes both how the agent searches and how it decides whether
evidence is sufficient for inclusion.
Figures [5](#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6.5 Learned Domain Judgment ‣ 6 Experiments on Harvey LAB ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")
and [6](#S6.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 6.5 Learned Domain Judgment ‣ 6 Experiments on Harvey LAB ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")
compare agents without learning and with the multi-learner components on
two test tasks, one per solver, illustrating two forms of learned
judgment: recognizing a concept across varied terminology, and applying
the right criteria for whether a candidate belongs in the answer.

#### 6.5.1 Searching by Meaning

In
Figure [5](#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6.5 Learned Domain Judgment ‣ 6 Experiments on Harvey LAB ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems"),
the task asks for the most recent signed M&A transaction containing a
no-shop covenant. Without learning, Qwen3.8-Flash first searches for the
literal term “no-shop.” It later finds covenants headed “Exclusivity”
and “No Solicitation,” but treats only a clause headed “No-Shop” as
decisive and selects an agreement signed on May 20, 2025. With the
learned components, the agent searches for “no-shop,” “Exclusivity,” and
“No Solicitation” from the start and reads each covenant by what it
restricts. It also excludes a later hotel purchase, which the firm’s
records file under Real Estate, and a letter of intent without a signed
definitive agreement. It identifies a qualifying transaction signed on
June 16, 2025.

The key difference is procedural: the learned agent maps the legal
concept to its plausible formulations and judges each candidate by its
substance rather than its heading.

#### 6.5.2 Deciding What Belongs in the Answer

In
Figure [6](#S6.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 6.5 Learned Domain Judgment ‣ 6 Experiments on Harvey LAB ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems"),
the task asks for all IP matters that resolved by settlement. Without
learning, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash identifies IP matters by subject-matter
keywords such as “patent” and “trade secret” and returns eight matters,
including a restrictive-covenant dispute that carried a trade-secret
claim. With the learned components, the agent first establishes scope
from engagement records, which name each matter’s responsible practice
group, and then checks each IP matter for an executed settlement. The
restrictive-covenant dispute is booked to Labor & Employment, so the
agent returns the seven qualifying matters. Qwen3.8-Flash makes the same
correction after learning.

This procedure separates two kinds of evidence that are easy to
conflate: evidence that a matter touches intellectual property and
evidence that the firm handled it as an IP matter. The improvement comes
from applying a more appropriate inclusion rule.

## 7 Conclusions

In this paper, we introduce the problem of building a recursively
self-improving foundation model system that improves its own
components—the model, knowledge repository, and harness—as well as its
learning process as it encounters new domain knowledge and requirements.

Recursa addresses this problem in two phases: bootstrapping builds
domain knowledge, and multi-agent learning from task experience refines
the knowledge repository of instructions, skills, and memory, without
relying on a stronger model to write the revisions. Our results on
Harvey LAB demonstrate that Recursa improves its own performance on
held-out tasks.

Extending recursive self-improvement to the foundation models and the
harness is ongoing work. Future work will also extend Recursa to other
domains such as finance, engineering, and the sciences.

## 8 Limitations

Recursa has shown promising results; however, it has several limitations
in addition to those discussed earlier, and users need to be aware of
them. First, the system’s performance relies on the quality and
availability of domain-specific corpora, which may be limited or
unavailable in certain domains. Second, the system requires substantial
computational resources for large language model inference and training,
which may limit its accessibility. Third, incorrect or biased data and
flaws in the underlying models can propagate through the learning
process, leading to unreliable or biased outcomes. Fourth, the
effectiveness of learning is contingent on the capability of the
underlying models, and we have not investigated the impact of model
limitations. Finally, our experiments have primarily focused on a
limited set of domains and may not capture the system’s performance
across all possible domains. For ethical and safety considerations,
Recursa autonomously explores software environments, executes programs,
and retains observed information in its memory, introducing potential
risks related to privacy and security. Our experiments have been
conducted in controlled sandbox environments with strict isolation and
no network access, except through controlled channels for model
inference and training, using only public datasets downloaded in
advance.

## Appendix B Revisions to the Firm Knowledge Rubrics

We use the Firm Knowledge tasks and rubrics of the Harvey LAB
repository ([Harvey AI, 2026](#bib.bib14)) at commit b22bccf.²² 2 Full
commit hash: b22bccffd2a496ffc871ffdd1514cde194034071. Each task is
graded against task-specific criteria, 2,623 in total across the 250
tasks. While analyzing failed criteria in our runs, we checked each
disputed criterion against the task statement and the source documents
in the corpus. We found 46 criteria in 30 tasks that conflict with one
or the other; 17 of these tasks are in the training split and 13 in the
test split. We revise a criterion only when the source documents support
the change, and leave unresolved candidates in their original form.
Revisions change criterion text only: task statements, criterion IDs,
the number of criteria, and deliverable requirements are unchanged, and
the other 220 tasks are identical to the original.

Table [5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Placeholder: the criterion contains an unexpanded placeholder. ‣ Appendix B Revisions to the Firm Knowledge Rubrics ‣ Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems")
lists the 46 revised criteria and labels each with one of five kinds of
issue.

##### Contradicts: the criterion contradicts the task statement.

These criteria measure something other than what the task asks. Q076
asks which cases _resulted_ in a royalty rate above 5%, but its criteria
count rates that were only asserted or proposed in litigation. The
settlement totals in Q118 and Q121 count only the cash portion of one
settlement while counting full consideration for the others, and Q110
requires subtotals over settlements below the task’s \$10 million
threshold. Q141 requires an answer that the executed agreement
contradicts without saying which source controls, and Q151 identifies
the deal as the one the firm most recently closed when the task asks for
the most recent signing. The revisions grade what the task asks.

##### Files: evidence is restricted to named files.

The task asks for a document that shows a fact, but the criterion
accepts only specific files. An answer that cites a different original
document establishing the same fact, often a more direct one such as the
executed agreement, fails. In Q011, for example, the criterion accepts
only an internal memo for the adopted EBITDA add-backs and rejects the
executed credit agreement, which lists the same add-backs. The revisions
keep the named files as examples and accept any document in the same
matter that directly establishes the fact.

##### Omits: the answer set omits qualifying items.

Precision criteria close the set of acceptable answers. When the set
omits a qualifying matter, an answer that correctly includes it fails.
Q193 asks for every matter where OFAC comes up, but its set follows a
literal acronym search and misses seven matters that name the Office of
Foreign Assets Control in full. The revisions add only the members that
the source documents establish.

##### Admits: the answer set admits excluded items.

When the set admits a matter that the task excludes, an incorrect answer
passes. The excluded matters fall outside the task’s practice area, as
in Q224 and Q235, where the task names the practice group that filed the
matter; its collateral, as in Q016, which excludes real-estate-secured
financings; its venue, as in Q205; or its time window, as in Q204. The
revisions remove only the members that the source documents exclude.

##### Placeholder: the criterion contains an unexpanded placeholder.

Q189 and Q190 refer to “\[same 37-entry set\]” and “\[15 qualifying
matters\]” instead of listing the matters, so the judge has no set to
check against. The revisions expand each placeholder into the matters
named in the task’s other criteria and in the original criterion,
without re-verifying them.

[TABLE]

Table 5: The 46 revised criteria in 30 Firm Knowledge tasks: the
original criterion, the revised criterion used for grading, and the
reason for the revision. Below each criterion ID, the label gives the
kind of error the revision corrects: _Contradicts_, the criterion
contradicts the task statement; _Files_, evidence is restricted to named
files; _Omits_, the answer set omits qualifying items; _Admits_, the
answer set admits excluded items; _Placeholder_, an unexpanded
placeholder.
